passages.t: Not by might nor by power, but by the Spirit
passages.happening:
The angel wakes Zechariah like a man woken from sleep (verse 1). He sees a solid gold lampstand with a bowl on top and seven lamps, and two olive trees beside it, one on each side (verses 2-3). He asks what they are (verse 4).

The answer is a word to Zerubbabel: ‘Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit, says the LORD of Hosts’ (verse 6). The great mountain before Zerubbabel will become a plain, and he will bring out the capstone with shouts of grace (verse 7). ‘The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house, and his hands will complete it’ (verse 9). ‘For who has despised the day of small things?’ (verse 10). The seven eyes of the LORD, which scan the whole earth, will rejoice when they see the plumb line in Zerubbabel's hand.
passages.hearers:
Zerubbabel had laid the temple's foundation years before and resumed the work in 520 BC. About this time the Persian governor of the province, Tattenai, came to ask who had authorized the building and wrote to Darius. Darius searched the archives, found Cyrus's decree, and ordered the work to continue with royal funds. The great mountain may be the obstacles in general, the heap of rubble on the site, or the opposition.

The lampstand was familiar temple furniture: the tabernacle had one golden lampstand with seven lamps. This one is different. A bowl on top feeds the lamps, and living olive trees supply it directly, so no human hand has to refill it. The picture says that the work will be supplied by God's Spirit, not by human strength. The capstone and the plumb line belong to the rites of laying and finishing a building.

The day of small things was the discouraging present: a small temple, a small province, a small people. God says not to despise it.
passages.later: Ezra tells of Tattenai's letter and Darius's reply (Ezra 5:3 to 6:12). The tabernacle's lampstand had seven lamps (Exodus 25:31-37).
passages.asks: The temple would be finished by God's Spirit, not by might or power. Ask what you are trying to do by your own strength alone. And ask what small beginning in your life you have been tempted to despise.

passages.happening:
Zechariah asks about the two olive trees on the right and left of the lampstand (verse 11), and the two olive branches beside the gold pipes from which the golden oil pours (verse 12). The angel asks whether he does not know, and he says he does not (verse 13).

The angel answers, “These are the two anointed ones who are standing beside the Lord of all the earth” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Olive oil was the fuel of every lamp and also the oil used to anoint priests and kings. The Hebrew phrase behind anointed ones is literally sons of fresh oil.

The vision began with the lampstand, explained in verses 6 to 10, and comes back at the end to the trees that supply it. The two figures stand beside the Lord of all the earth, as servants ready to do his will.
passages.later: The tabernacle's lamps burned on ‘pure oil of pressed olives for the light’ (Exodus 27:20), and the priests were anointed with oil to serve: ‘Anoint Aaron and his sons and consecrate them to serve Me as priests’ (Exodus 30:30).
passages.hard:
Who are the two olive trees, the two anointed ones?

Most interpreters take them to be Joshua and Zerubbabel, the priest and the governor who lead the community, since chapter 3 concerned Joshua and this chapter concerns Zerubbabel. Some scholars point out that neither man is known to have been formally anointed, and that the unusual phrase sons of fresh oil may describe them as channels of God's supply rather than anointed officials. A few have suggested the prophets Haggai and Zechariah. Christian readers have sometimes taken the two trees as the two Testaments or as two witnesses still to come. The chapter's own emphasis falls less on who they are than on the source of their oil.
passages.asks: The olive trees supply the lamp without human hands. Ask where you need to rely on what God supplies rather than on what you can produce. And ask whom God may have set beside you to share the work.
